name: PINNs and neural operators learn PDE solution maps
summary: Physics-informed networks put the residual of the differential equation and its boundary conditions into the loss. Neural operators (DeepONet, Fourier neural operator) learn the whole solution map f↦u, a nonlinear generalization of the Green's-function integral operator, written as a kernel integral or a spectral multiplier.
map: u(x)=\int G(x,x')f(x')dx'\to u=\mathcal G_\theta[f];\ \mathcal L\supset\lambda\|\mathcal N u_\theta\|^2
breaks: Unlike a Green's function, the learned operator carries no guarantee of causality, conservation or accuracy outside its training distribution.
sources: Raissi, Perdikaris & Karniadakis (2019). "Physics-informed neural networks: A deep learning framework for solving forward and inverse problems involving nonlinear partial differential equations". *J. Comput. Phys.* 378, 686. [doi:10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045)

name: Learned likelihood ratios and simulation-based inference
summary: A classifier trained to separate samples from two hypotheses learns their likelihood ratio, the Neyman–Pearson optimal test statistic. Neural density estimators learn posteriors straight from simulators, so frequentist and Bayesian inference work even when the likelihood is intractable, as in collider, cosmology and gravitational-wave analyses.
sources: Carleo et al. (2019). "Machine learning and the physical sciences". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 045002. [arXiv:1903.10563](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.10563)

name: Equivariant networks built from group representations
summary: Group-equivariant networks build symmetry into the architecture. Convolutions are generalized to E(3)/SE(3) or lattice gauge groups, and features transform in irreducible representations coupled by Clebsch–Gordan products. They are used in molecular force fields and in gauge-equivariant flows for lattice QCD, where they need far less data and keep the symmetry exact.
sources: Carleo et al. (2019). "Machine learning and the physical sciences". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 91, 045002. [arXiv:1903.10563](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.10563)

name: Buckingham π as a prior for symbolic regression
summary: Symbolic-regression systems that rediscover physical laws (e.g. AI Feynman) apply the π theorem first, cutting the number of independent variables before searching formula space. Surrogates fed dimensionless groups generalize across scales, the same way similarity lets wind-tunnel results transfer.
sources: Buckingham (1914). "On Physically Similar Systems; Illustrations of the Use of Dimensional Equations". *Phys. Rev.* 4, 345. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.4.345](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.4.345)

name: Which conservation laws an MD run actually keeps
summary: Pair forces obey Newton's third law, so velocity Verlet conserves total momentum to round-off. Periodic boundaries break rotational invariance, so angular momentum is not conserved. Nosé–Hoover thermostats break energy conservation on purpose but conserve an extended Hamiltonian, and drift in any of these quantities flags a bug or too large a time step.
sources: Verlet (1967). "Computer 'Experiments' on Classical Fluids. I. Thermodynamical Properties of Lennard-Jones Molecules". *Phys. Rev.* 159, 98. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.159.98](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.159.98)

name: Monte Carlo as a product of Los Alamos big science
summary: Ulam, von Neumann and Metropolis developed statistical sampling for neutron-transport problems at Los Alamos, and the 1953 Metropolis algorithm ran on the MANIAC computer. Simulation, a third way between theory and experiment, grew directly out of wartime big science and the first electronic computers.
sources: Metropolis et al. (1953). "Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines". *J. Chem. Phys.* 21, 1087. [doi:10.1063/1.1699114](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1699114)

name: Sign problem: deforming path integrals into ℂ
summary: With complex weights (finite-density QCD, real-time path integrals, frustrated fermions), importance sampling breaks down. Picard–Lefschetz theory moves the integration contour onto steepest-descent thimbles where the phase is constant, and complex Langevin complexifies the fields. Both carry saddle-point methods from complex analysis into Monte Carlo.
breaks: Thimbles still interfere with each other, and complex Langevin can converge to wrong answers. The general sign problem is NP-hard, so these are only partial cures.

name: Feynman–Kac: random walks solve diffusion-type PDEs
summary: The Feynman–Kac formula writes the solution of the imaginary-time Schrödinger or diffusion equation, a Green's-function propagator, as an average over Brownian paths. Diffusion and Green's-function quantum Monte Carlo use it to project out ground states, and walk-on-spheres solves Laplace and Poisson problems.
breaks: For fermions the walkers' weights change sign, so the method needs a fixed-node approximation.

name: MCMC: Boltzmann samplers became posterior samplers
summary: Set $E(\theta)=-\ln[L(D|\theta)\pi(\theta)]$ and $\beta=1$, and the Metropolis chain, built for Boltzmann weights, samples the Bayesian posterior. This drives cosmological and global particle-physics fits. Hybrid Monte Carlo, invented for lattice QCD, became the default sampler in Bayesian software (Stan's NUTS is a variant).
sources: Metropolis et al. (1953). "Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines". *J. Chem. Phys.* 21, 1087. [doi:10.1063/1.1699114](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1699114)

name: Monte Carlo propagation of distributions (GUM-S1)
summary: When the measurement model is strongly nonlinear or the inputs are non-Gaussian, the first-order law of propagation fails. GUM Supplement 1 replaces it with Monte Carlo: sample the input distributions, push each sample through the model and read the coverage interval off the output distribution.
map: u_c^2(y)=\mathbf c^TV_x\mathbf c\ \to\ y^{(k)}=f(x^{(k)}),\ x^{(k)}\sim p(x)

name: Analytic PDE structure underpins numerical schemes
summary: The same boundary- and initial-value problems are solved analytically (separation of variables, Sturm–Liouville eigenbases, Green's functions) and numerically. Spectral methods expand in those eigenfunctions, finite elements are Galerkin projections of the weak form, and well-posedness reappears as numerical stability.

name: Discrete Noether theorem for variational integrators
summary: Integrators derived from a discrete action inherit its symmetries: a discrete Noether theorem makes them conserve the corresponding momenta exactly. Because they are symplectic, they also conserve a modified Hamiltonian over exponentially long times, so energy errors stay bounded instead of drifting.
map: \tilde H=H+\Delta t^pH_{p+1}+\dots;\ |H(t)-H(0)|=O(\Delta t^p)\ \text{for}\ t\lesssim e^{c/\Delta t}
breaks: Energy itself is not exactly conserved, because a fixed step breaks continuous time-translation symmetry. Adaptive step sizes destroy the symplectic guarantee.

name: MPS as iterated SVD; bond dimension bounds entanglement
summary: A matrix product state is built from repeated Schmidt (singular-value) decompositions of the state vector. Keeping the χ largest singular values is the optimal low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young), χ caps the bipartite entanglement, and DMRG is a Lanczos-type variational eigenproblem on this manifold.
breaks: Efficient only for area-law states. Volume-law states, such as those after long quenches, need χ exponential in system size.
sources: White (1992). "Density matrix formulation for quantum renormalization groups". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 69, 2863. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2863](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2863)
Schollwöck (2011). "The density-matrix renormalization group in the age of matrix product states". *Ann. Phys.* 326, 96. [arXiv:1008.3477](https://arxiv.org/abs/1008.3477)

name: Broken symmetry as the paradigm of emergence
summary: Anderson's 'More is different' uses spontaneous symmetry breaking as its central example of emergence: a ground state can lack the symmetry of the laws, and rigidity, order parameters and Goldstone modes follow. Philosophers debate whether this is genuine emergence, because strict SSB needs the infinite-volume limit.
sources: Anderson (1972). "More Is Different". *Science* 177, 393. [doi:10.1126/science.177.4047.393](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.177.4047.393)

name: SSB migrated from superconductivity to particle physics
summary: Nambu (1960–61) took the BCS ground state and the puzzle of its gauge invariance as the template for spontaneously broken symmetry in particle physics, and Goldstone generalized the massless mode. Anderson (1963) and Englert–Brout, Higgs and Guralnik–Hagen–Kibble (1964) then showed how gauge fields evade it, a textbook case of an idea crossing from condensed matter.
sources: Nambu (1960). "Quasi-Particles and Gauge Invariance in the Theory of Superconductivity". *Phys. Rev.* 117, 648. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.117.648](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.117.648)
Goldstone (1961). "Field theories with Superconductor solutions". *Nuovo Cimento* 19, 154. [doi:10.1007/BF02812722](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02812722)

name: Gleason and Kochen–Specker: Born rule and contextuality
summary: Two interpretive questions are settled as theorems about Hilbert space. Gleason: for dim ≥ 3, every additive probability measure on projectors has the form Tr(ρP), so the Born rule follows from the lattice of subspaces. Kochen–Specker: no noncontextual assignment of definite values to all projectors exists, which constrains hidden-variable interpretations.

name: Hole argument: diffeomorphisms and gauge redundancy
summary: General covariance makes a metric and its pullback by a diffeomorphism physically equivalent. Einstein's hole argument turns this into the substantivalism–relationism debate, settled in practice by treating only diffeomorphism-invariant quantities as observable. The fibre-bundle view of gauge fields gets the same reading: only holonomies and curvature are physical ('gauge as redundancy').

name: Arrow of time vs. microscopic T violation
summary: The fundamental laws are T-invariant except for the weak interaction, where CP violation together with CPT implies T violation. Philosophers of physics stress that this small, Hamiltonian-level asymmetry does not explain the thermodynamic arrow, which instead traces to a low-entropy initial state (the past hypothesis).

name: Are c, ħ, G fundamental or just unit conversions?
summary: Natural units set c, ħ, G and k_B to 1, which shows that dimensionful constants act largely as unit conversions. Only dimensionless combinations such as α or m_p/m_e are unit-independent and can be meaningfully tested for variation. How many dimensionful constants are fundamental (three, two or none) is still debated, notably in the Duff–Okun–Veneziano 'trialogue'.

name: Point vs. set paradigms of measurement in learning
summary: PER finds that many students treat a single reading as 'the true value' (point paradigm) instead of seeing a measurement as a distribution summarized by a best estimate and an uncertainty (set paradigm). Lab curricula built on the GUM framework target this shift, so uncertainty is both a metrology topic and a documented learning difficulty.

name: Symmetry acts through linear representations
summary: Symmetry groups act on state spaces through linear, usually unitary or projective, representations. Group theory in physics therefore runs on the mathematical-methods toolkit: Hilbert-space operators and eigenproblems, special functions as representation bases, and differential geometry for Lie groups and gauge connections.
sources: Wigner (1939). "On Unitary Representations of the Inhomogeneous Lorentz Group". *Ann. Math.* 40, 149. [doi:10.2307/1968551](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968551)

name: Causal transfer functions: Kramers–Kronig, Bode, Nyquist
summary: A causal, stable signal chain has a transfer function analytic in a half-plane, so its gain and phase are tied together (Kramers–Kronig, Bode). The Nyquist criterion, the argument principle applied to the loop gain, decides whether a feedback amplifier or phase-locked loop oscillates. Bode's relations limit how much feedback a front end can have over a given bandwidth.

name: Special functions as representation matrix elements
summary: The classical special functions are matrix elements or bases of Lie-group representations: spherical harmonics and Legendre polynomials for SO(3), Wigner D-functions for SU(2), Bessel functions for the Euclidean group E(2), Hermite functions for the Heisenberg–Weyl group. Their addition theorems, recursions and orthogonality follow from group multiplication, ladder operators and Peter–Weyl.

name: Lie groups were invented to integrate ODEs
summary: Sophus Lie built the theory of continuous groups in the 1870s to do for differential equations what Galois theory did for polynomials. Each one-parameter point symmetry lowers an ODE's order by one, and symmetry reductions of PDEs give similarity solutions and separable coordinates. The algebraic core of that programme became the Lie theory physics uses today.

name: Self-similar solutions: scaling turns PDEs into ODEs
summary: When a problem has no intrinsic scale, dimensional analysis forces a similarity form that reduces the PDE to an ODE: the heat kernel, the Blasius boundary layer, the Taylor–Sedov blast wave. In second-kind (intermediate) asymptotics the exponents are not fixed by dimensions and come out as eigenvalues of the reduced problem.
sources: Buckingham (1914). "On Physically Similar Systems; Illustrations of the Use of Dimensional Equations". *Phys. Rev.* 4, 345. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.4.345](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.4.345)

name: Wigner's theorem: time reversal is antiunitary
summary: By Wigner's theorem every quantum symmetry is unitary or antiunitary, and time reversal must be antiunitary, T=UK. For half-integer spin T²=−1, so ψ and Tψ are orthogonal with equal energy, and every level of a T-invariant Hamiltonian is at least doubly degenerate (Kramers). The same antiunitary structure fixes the random-matrix and topological symmetry classes.

name: Schur's lemma: symmetry dictates degeneracy
summary: By Schur's lemma, an operator that commutes with an irreducible representation is a multiple of the identity on it. Symmetry-protected degeneracies therefore equal irrep dimensions (2l+1 for SO(3)) and eigenbases are labelled by Casimirs. The Wigner–Eckart theorem reduces tensor-operator matrix elements to Clebsch–Gordan coefficients, which gives the selection rules.

name: Gauge fields are Lie-algebra-valued connections
summary: A Lie group is a manifold whose tangent space at the identity is its Lie algebra. A gauge potential is a Lie-algebra-valued connection one-form on a principal G-bundle, and the field strength is its curvature. Yang–Mills theory and gravity therefore share connections, parallel transport and curvature (holonomy = Wilson loop).

breaks: Gravity's connection is soldered to the tangent bundle and fixed by the metric, and its action is not of Yang–Mills type.

name: Killing vectors turn ∇·T=0 into conserved charges
summary: In curved spacetime, ∇_μT^{μν}=0 gives no integral conservation law by itself. Only an isometry (a Killing vector ξ) makes J^μ=T^{μν}ξ_ν a conserved current with a global charge, which is Noether's theorem in geometric form. The contracted Bianchi identity is the identity Noether's second theorem attaches to diffeomorphism invariance, which resolved Hilbert and Klein's 1918 energy puzzle.

name: Metrology: value × unit ± uncertainty, traceable to SI
summary: A complete measurement result is a number times an SI unit plus an uncertainty. Traceability links any instrument through an unbroken calibration chain to the unit definitions, and since the 2019 redefinition that chain ends at exact constants rather than artefacts.
sources: Stock et al. (2019). "The revision of the SI—the result of three decades of progress in metrology". *Metrologia* 56, 022001. [doi:10.1088/1681-7575/ab0013](https://doi.org/10.1088/1681-7575/ab0013)

name: EDM and CPT tests as noise-limited precision measurements
summary: Two kinds of experiment are limited by sensor noise: searches for permanent electric dipole moments (the neutron, the electron in polar molecules), which would violate P and T, and CPT tests comparing particles with antiparticles in Penning traps or by antihydrogen spectroscopy. Their reach on new CP violation is set by magnetometry, spin-precession readout and cryogenic trap techniques.
map: H=-(\mu\mathbf B+d\mathbf E)\cdot\hat{\mathbf S},\ \delta d\sim\frac{\hbar}{2E\tau\sqrt N}

name: Josephson and QHE standards realize volt, ohm, kilogram
summary: Quantum electrical devices turn the exact h and e into units: Josephson arrays give voltages nf/K_J and quantum Hall bars give resistances R_K/i. The Kibble balance balances mechanical against electrical power measured with both, which realizes the 2019 kilogram from h.
sources: Robinson & Schlamminger (2016). "The watt or Kibble balance: a technique for implementing the new SI definition of the unit of mass". *Metrologia* 53, A46. [doi:10.1088/0026-1394/53/5/A46](https://doi.org/10.1088/0026-1394/53/5/A46)
Stock et al. (2019). "The revision of the SI—the result of three decades of progress in metrology". *Metrologia* 56, 022001. [doi:10.1088/1681-7575/ab0013](https://doi.org/10.1088/1681-7575/ab0013)

name: CODATA adjustment as generalized least squares
summary: CODATA recommended values come from a linearized generalized least-squares fit of well over a hundred correlated experimental and theoretical inputs. Consistency is checked with the Birge ratio and normalized residuals, and discrepant inputs get expanded uncertainties. The roughly 5σ disagreement between the Cs and Rb atom-recoil values of α is the kind of tension this step has to absorb.
sources: Tiesinga et al. (2021). "CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants: 2018". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 93, 025010. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010)

Morel et al. (2020). "Determination of the fine-structure constant with an accuracy of 81 parts per trillion". *Nature* 588, 61. [doi:10.1038/s41586-020-2964-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2964-7)

name: Unit realizations carry GUM uncertainty budgets
summary: Each realization of an SI unit reports a GUM budget of Type A and Type B components: the Kibble balance or silicon-sphere XRCD for the kilogram, acoustic-gas or Johnson-noise thermometry for the kelvin. Traceability carries that uncertainty down the calibration chain into every measurement.
sources: Robinson & Schlamminger (2016). "The watt or Kibble balance: a technique for implementing the new SI definition of the unit of mass". *Metrologia* 53, A46. [doi:10.1088/0026-1394/53/5/A46](https://doi.org/10.1088/0026-1394/53/5/A46)

name: CODATA uncertainties, correlations and exact constants
summary: CODATA values carry standard uncertainties plus a correlation matrix, because many constants derive from shared inputs. Since 2019 h, e, k and N_A are exact, so their former uncertainty now sits in μ0, ε0, the molar mass constant and the mass of the old prototype kilogram.
sources: Tiesinga et al. (2021). "CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants: 2018". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 93, 025010. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.93.025010)

name: Energy-based neural PDE solvers (Deep Ritz)
summary: Networks can minimize the variational energy of a mechanics problem instead of a residual, turning the principle of minimum potential energy into the training objective.
sources: Samaniego et al. (2020). "An energy approach to the solution of partial differential equations in computational mechanics via machine learning: Concepts, implementation and applications". *Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Eng.* 362, 112790. [arXiv:1908.10407](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10407)

name: Physics-informed networks for Navier–Stokes
summary: PINNs penalize the Navier–Stokes residual in the loss to reconstruct velocity and pressure from sparse data; flow problems are the main testbed for scientific-ML surrogates.
sources: Cai et al. (2021). "Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for fluid mechanics: a review". *Acta Mech. Sin.* 37, 1727. [arXiv:2105.09506](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.09506)

Raissi, Perdikaris & Karniadakis (2019). "Physics-informed neural networks: A deep learning framework for solving forward and inverse problems involving nonlinear partial differential equations". *J. Comput. Phys.* 378, 686. [doi:10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045)

name: Molecular dynamics integrates Hamilton's equations
summary: MD is numerical Hamiltonian mechanics for N particles; Nosé's extended Hamiltonian adds a thermostat variable so that the deterministic flow samples the canonical ensemble.
sources: Verlet (1967). "Computer 'Experiments' on Classical Fluids. I. Thermodynamical Properties of Lennard-Jones Molecules". *Phys. Rev.* 159, 98. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.159.98](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.159.98)
Nosé (1984). "A unified formulation of the constant temperature molecular dynamics methods". *J. Chem. Phys.* 81, 511. [doi:10.1063/1.447334](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.447334)

name: Lyapunov instability underlies MD ergodicity
summary: Many-particle MD trajectories are chaotic with positive Lyapunov exponents, so individual trajectories are irreproducible after picoseconds while time averages converge to ensemble averages; chaos is what makes MD statistics robust.

name: Hamiltonian (hybrid) Monte Carlo
summary: HMC proposes moves by integrating fictitious Hamiltonian dynamics with leapfrog; time reversibility and Liouville volume preservation make the Metropolis correction exact.

name: Symplectic integrators ↔ Hamiltonian flow
summary: Leapfrog/Verlet and other symplectic schemes are exact flows of a nearby 'shadow' Hamiltonian, so they preserve phase-space volume and show no secular energy drift; the integrator inherits the symplectic structure of Hamilton's equations.
breaks: Backward-error bound holds only for fixed step size; adaptive steps or dissipation destroy the shadow Hamiltonian.
sources: Verlet (1967). "Computer 'Experiments' on Classical Fluids. I. Thermodynamical Properties of Lennard-Jones Molecules". *Phys. Rev.* 159, 98. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.159.98](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.159.98)

name: Variational integrators and Ritz–Galerkin
summary: Discretizing the action rather than the equations gives variational integrators that are automatically symplectic and momentum-conserving (discrete Noether); finite elements are Ritz minimization of an energy functional.

name: Finite elements born in structural elasticity
summary: The finite element method grew out of structural and elasticity analysis (Courant's 1943 variational triangles, 1950s aircraft stress analysis) and is a Ritz–Galerkin minimization of the elastic energy.

name: DNS and spectral solvers ↔ turbulence
summary: Direct numerical simulation must resolve from the integral scale L down to the Kolmogorov scale η, so grid points grow as Re^{9/4}; pseudospectral FFT methods and LES closures are the workhorses of turbulence research.

name: N-body integrators ↔ celestial mechanics
summary: Long-term Solar System integrations use symplectic map methods (Wisdom–Holman splitting into Kepler drift plus interaction kick) and regularization for close encounters.
map: H=H_{\rm Kep}+H_{\rm int},\ \ e^{hL_H}\approx e^{\frac h2L_{\rm int}}e^{hL_{\rm Kep}}e^{\frac h2L_{\rm int}}

name: Lyapunov spectra and shadowing in numerics
summary: Lyapunov exponents are computed by tangent-map integration with repeated QR (Gram–Schmidt) reorthonormalization; the shadowing lemma justifies trusting chaotic numerical orbits statistically even though each diverges from the true one.

name: Standard map = leapfrog kicked rotor
summary: Chirikov's standard map is the symplectic-Euler discretization of a pendulum and the exact flow of the kicked rotor; KAM theory explains why symplectic integrators keep invariant tori and stay stable for exponentially long times.
breaks: Correspondence with the continuous pendulum holds only for small step K; for K≳1 the map's global chaos is a discretization artifact.

name: Rutherford scattering discovered the nucleus
summary: Rutherford's classical Coulomb-orbit cross-section, fitted to Geiger–Marsden α data, revealed the atomic nucleus; the same formula happens to be exact in quantum mechanics.
sources: Rutherford (1911). "The scattering of α and β particles by matter and the structure of the atom". *Phil. Mag.* 21, 669. [doi:10.1080/14786440508637080](https://doi.org/10.1080/14786440508637080)

name: Liouville, recurrence and the arrow of time
summary: Time-reversal-invariant Hamiltonian flow preserves phase-space volume, so fine-grained Gibbs entropy is constant and Poincaré recurrence holds; irreversibility needs coarse-graining plus a low-entropy past.

name: Force Concept Inventory ↔ Newton's laws
summary: Newton's three laws are the content probed by the Force Concept Inventory; PER shows students hold impetus-like preconceptions, and interactive engagement roughly doubles the normalized gain.
sources: Hestenes, Wells & Swackhamer (1992). "Force concept inventory". *Phys. Teach.* 30, 141. [doi:10.1119/1.2343497](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.2343497)

Hake (1998). "Interactive-engagement versus traditional methods: A six-thousand-student survey of mechanics test data for introductory physics courses". *Am. J. Phys.* 66, 64. [doi:10.1119/1.18809](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.18809)

name: Conformal maps for 2D potential flow and lift
summary: Planar irrotational incompressible flow is an analytic complex potential; Joukowski conformal maps generate airfoils and the Blasius contour integral gives the Kutta–Joukowski lift.

name: Small divisors and analytic estimates in KAM
summary: Lindstedt perturbation series diverge because of small denominators k·ω; KAM proves torus survival for Diophantine frequencies by Newton iteration with Cauchy estimates on shrinking complex analyticity strips.

name: Inverse scattering via analytic scattering data
summary: The inverse scattering transform solves KdV and NLS by mapping initial data to scattering data analytic in the spectral parameter, reconstructed through a Riemann–Hilbert (Gelfand–Levitan) problem; solitons are bound-state poles.

name: Damped oscillator response ↔ causality and Kramers–Kronig
summary: The driven damped oscillator's susceptibility has poles only in the lower half ω-plane because the response is causal, so its real and imaginary parts obey Kramers–Kronig; its impulse response is the retarded Green's function.

name: Hamilton–Jacobi PDE ↔ method of characteristics
summary: The Hamilton–Jacobi equation is a first-order nonlinear PDE whose characteristics are exactly Hamilton's equations; complete integrals give generating functions of canonical transformations.

name: Stokeslet = Green's function of Stokes flow
summary: The Oseen tensor (Stokeslet) is the Green's function of the Stokes equations; boundary-integral, slender-body and hydrodynamic-interaction methods superpose it.

name: Acoustic waves ↔ retarded Green's function
summary: Sound radiated by sources is the source convolved with the retarded Green's function of the wave equation; Huygens' sharp-front principle holds in odd spatial dimensions.

name: Floquet theory of the Mathieu equation
summary: Parametric resonance is governed by Floquet–Hill theory of linear ODEs with periodic coefficients; Mathieu characteristic exponents define the instability tongues near ω = 2ω₀/n.

name: Poisson brackets ↔ commutators; Koopman–von Neumann
summary: Dirac's rule {f,g} → [f̂,ĝ]/iħ maps Hamiltonian mechanics onto Hilbert-space operators; conversely Koopman–von Neumann write classical mechanics as unitary evolution on L²(phase space).
breaks: Groenewold–van Hove: no quantization map preserves all brackets beyond quadratic polynomials.

name: Normal modes = generalized eigenproblem
summary: Small oscillations about equilibrium reduce to the symmetric generalized eigenproblem Kv = ω²Mv; normal modes are the orthogonal eigenvectors guaranteed by the spectral theorem.

name: Principal axes = spectral theorem for the inertia tensor
summary: The inertia tensor is real symmetric, so it has orthogonal eigenvectors (principal axes) and real eigenvalues (principal moments); rotational kinetic energy is diagonal in that basis.

name: Phase space as a symplectic manifold
summary: Phase space is the cotangent bundle T*Q with symplectic 2-form ω = dp∧dq; Hamilton's equations are ι_X ω = dH, Poisson brackets come from ω^{-1}, and Liouville's theorem is conservation of the volume form ω^n.

name: Strain compatibility = flat metric; defects = torsion and curvature
summary: Saint-Venant compatibility is the vanishing Riemann tensor of the deformed metric g = δ + 2ε; in the geometric theory of defects dislocations are torsion and disclinations curvature of a material connection.

name: Fictitious forces as connection coefficients
summary: Coriolis and centrifugal forces are the Christoffel symbols of rotating coordinates in flat space; writing Newton's law covariantly prefigures the equivalence principle.

name: Resonant sensors: Q, bandwidth and thermal force noise
summary: Mechanical and electrical resonators used as sensors are driven damped oscillators; Q sets the bandwidth f₀/Q and the lock-in readout, and via fluctuation–dissipation the thermal force-noise floor.

name: Least squares born from orbit determination
summary: Gauss developed least squares and the normal error law to recover the orbit of Ceres (1801–1809); χ² fitting of orbital elements remains the template for parameter estimation.

name: Kepler's hidden SO(4) and the Runge–Lenz vector
summary: The conserved Laplace–Runge–Lenz vector together with L generates SO(4) for bound Kepler orbits, explaining closed ellipses (Bertrand) and, once quantized, the n² degeneracy of hydrogen (Pauli 1926).

name: KdV hierarchies ↔ infinite-dimensional Lie algebras
summary: Integrable soliton equations come in hierarchies attached to Kac–Moody algebras (Drinfeld–Sokolov); the Lax pair is a flat connection in a loop algebra and tau functions carry representations of infinite-dimensional groups.
sources: Drinfeld & Sokolov (1984). "Lie algebras and equations of Korteweg-de Vries type". *J. Sov. Math.* 30, 1975. [doi:10.1007/bf02105860](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02105860)
Jimbo & Miwa (1983). "Solitons and Infinite Dimensional Lie Algebras". *Publ. RIMS Kyoto* 19, 943. [doi:10.2977/prims/1195182017](https://doi.org/10.2977/prims/1195182017)

name: Rotation group SO(3) ↔ rigid-body motion
summary: A rigid body's configuration space is SO(3); Euler's equations are the Lie–Poisson equations on so(3)*, and the inertia tensor defines a left-invariant metric whose geodesics are torque-free motions.

name: Invariance of the action → Noether currents
summary: Noether's theorem is a statement about the variational principle: a continuous transformation leaving the action invariant up to a boundary term yields a conserved quantity; cyclic coordinates are the simplest case.
map: \delta L=\frac{dK}{dt}\Rightarrow Q=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\delta q-K,\ \dot Q=0
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)

name: Kelvin circulation from particle-relabelling symmetry
summary: In the Lagrangian (Euler–Poincaré) formulation of ideal fluids, invariance under relabelling of fluid particles is a Noether symmetry whose charge is circulation; Kelvin's theorem and potential-vorticity conservation follow.
breaks: Exact only for ideal barotropic fluids; viscosity and baroclinic torques break it.

name: Newtonian mechanics as symmetry consequences
summary: The Galilean symmetry group of Newtonian mechanics (translations, rotations, boosts) fixes its conserved quantities; the Galilean boost charge gives uniform centre-of-mass motion.
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)

name: Noether's theorem ↔ energy, momentum, angular momentum
summary: The conservation laws of Newtonian mechanics are the Noether charges of time translation, space translation and rotation invariance of the action.
map: \partial L/\partial t=0\Rightarrow E=\dot q\,\partial L/\partial\dot q-L\ \text{conserved}
sources: Noether (1918; English translation 1971). "Invariant variation problems". *Transport Theory Stat. Phys.* 1, 186. [doi:10.1080/00411457108231446](https://doi.org/10.1080/00411457108231446)

name: Integrability = enough conserved charges in involution
summary: Liouville–Arnold integrability needs n Poisson-commuting conserved quantities; KdV has infinitely many, generated by commuting symmetry flows, which is why solitons survive collisions.

name: Elasticity as the Goldstone theory of broken translations
summary: A crystal breaks continuous translations; continuum elasticity is the effective theory of the corresponding Goldstone fields (displacements), and its sound waves are the Goldstone modes.
breaks: Broken rotations give no independent Goldstone modes (inverse Higgs); amorphous solids are elastic without long-range order.

name: Pitchfork bifurcation = Landau symmetry breaking
summary: The normal form of a Z2-symmetric pitchfork is gradient flow on a φ⁴ potential; the supercritical branch is mean-field spontaneous symmetry breaking with exponent 1/2.
breaks: No fluctuations or thermodynamic limit, so only mean-field exponents; Hopf bifurcations break time translation rather than an internal symmetry.

name: Kuramoto sync and Turing patterns as symmetry breaking
summary: Kuramoto synchronization is a U(1)-breaking transition with order parameter re^{iψ} and mean-field exponent 1/2; Turing patterns spontaneously break translation symmetry.
breaks: Driven-dissipative attractors with no free energy or detailed balance; the phase mode diffuses rather than propagating, and noise can restore the symmetry.

name: Galileo's square–cube law
summary: Galileo's 1638 argument that beam strength scales as L² while weight scales as L³ is the first scaling law and limits the size of animals and structures; Euler buckling follows the same logic.

name: Buckingham π ↔ Reynolds similarity
summary: Dimensional analysis reduces drag and flow problems to functions of a few dimensionless groups (Re, Ma, Fr), which is the basis of wind-tunnel scaling and dynamic similarity.
sources: Buckingham (1914). "On Physically Similar Systems; Illustrations of the Use of Dimensional Equations". *Phys. Rev.* 4, 345. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.4.345](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.4.345)

name: Re ≪ 1 regime and the scallop theorem
summary: At Re ≪ 1 inertia drops out and Stokes flow is linear and instantaneous, so reciprocal strokes give no net swimming (Purcell's scallop theorem); scaling arguments set what microswimmers can do.
sources: Purcell (1977). "Life at low Reynolds number". *Am. J. Phys.* 45, 3. [doi:10.1119/1.10903](https://doi.org/10.1119/1.10903)

name: Kolmogorov 1941 from dimensional analysis
summary: If the inertial range depends only on the dissipation rate ε and wavenumber k, dimensional analysis fixes the −5/3 spectrum and the Kolmogorov scale; intermittency corrections are the anomalous part beyond dimensional reasoning.

name: Photonic neural-network hardware and ML inverse design
summary: Any N×N unitary factorizes into a mesh of Mach–Zehnder interferometers (Reck and Clements decompositions). Programmable silicon-photonic meshes can therefore perform the matrix–vector products of neural-network inference optically. In the other direction, adjoint-gradient and neural-network inverse design produce non-intuitive waveguide, coupler and metasurface geometries.

name: Ewald summation: electrostatics on a periodic lattice
summary: Periodic simulations need the Coulomb energy of an infinite lattice of images, a conditionally convergent sum. Ewald splits 1/r into a short-range erfc part summed in real space and a smooth part summed in Fourier space. The leftover surface-dipole term depends on the dielectric condition at infinity; tin-foil boundaries (ε'=∞) are the usual choice.

name: Monte Carlo radiative transfer through turbid media
summary: Multiple scattering of light in clouds, tissue and dust is simulated as random walks of photon packets. Free paths are drawn from the extinction coefficient and scattering angles from a Mie or Henyey–Greenstein phase function. This solves the radiative transfer equation statistically where the diffusion approximation fails.
sources: Mie (1908). "Beiträge zur Optik trüber Medien, speziell kolloidaler Metallösungen". *Ann. Phys.* 330, 377. [doi:10.1002/andp.19083300302](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19083300302)

name: Yee's FDTD scheme for Maxwell's curl equations
summary: The finite-difference time-domain method staggers E and H by half a cell in space and half a step in time (leapfrog). The discrete curls then conserve the discrete divergence of B exactly, and of D given charge conservation, a discrete-exterior-calculus structure. Stability obeys the CFL bound. FDTD and edge-element finite elements are the workhorses of photonics and antenna design.

name: Split-step Fourier solution of the fibre NLSE
summary: Pulse propagation in a Kerr fibre obeys the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, solved by operator splitting. Dispersion is applied exactly in the Fourier domain and self-phase modulation in the time domain; Strang splitting makes the scheme second order. This norm-preserving pseudospectral method also underlies Lugiato–Lefever simulations of Kerr combs and solitons.

name: Maxwell's unification and the speed of light
summary: With the displacement current, Maxwell (1865) derived transverse waves travelling at 1/√(ε₀μ₀). That speed matched both Weber and Kohlrausch's measured ratio of electromagnetic to electrostatic units and the speed of light, so light became an electromagnetic wave. Hertz's 1887–88 experiments confirmed it, making this the archetype of unification in physics.
sources: Maxwell (1865). "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field". *Phil. Trans. R. Soc.* 155, 459. [doi:10.1098/rstl.1865.0008](https://doi.org/10.1098/rstl.1865.0008)

name: Electrodynamics of moving bodies gave special relativity
summary: Einstein's 1905 paper opens with the magnet–conductor asymmetry of Maxwell–Lorentz electrodynamics. He resolved it by making the Lorentz transformations, which already leave Maxwell's equations invariant, the kinematics of space and time. Minkowski's 1908 tensor form then made E and B frame-dependent parts of one object, so relativity grew out of electrodynamics rather than mechanics.
sources: Einstein (1905). "Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper". *Ann. Phys.* 322, 891. [doi:10.1002/andp.19053221004](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053221004)

name: Are potentials real? Gauge and the Aharonov–Bohm effect
summary: The Aharonov–Bohm phase shows that charged quanta respond to A where B vanishes. This forces a choice: gauge-dependent potentials acting locally, gauge-invariant loop holonomies acting nonlocally, or nonlocal field interactions. It is the main test case for whether gauge symmetry is mere redundancy of description or physically significant.

name: Radiation reaction and consistency of classical ED
summary: The Abraham–Lorentz–Dirac equation for a radiating point charge is third order, with runaway solutions and pre-acceleration, and the point charge's self-energy diverges. Whether classical electrodynamics of point particles is even consistent, and how to read the reduced-order Landau–Lifshitz fix, is debated in philosophy of physics. Strong-field laser experiments now probe the same question.
sources: Dirac (1938). "Classical theory of radiating electrons". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 167, 148. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1938.0124](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0124)

name: Rays as the stationary-phase limit; Airy caustics
summary: Geometric optics is the stationary-phase asymptotics of the diffraction integral as k→∞: rays are the stationary points of the optical path. Where two rays merge, the method fails at a caustic. The intensity there follows the Airy function, as in Airy's rainbow theory, which is where catastrophe optics begins.

name: Conformal mapping for 2D electrostatics
summary: In two dimensions the potential is the real part of an analytic complex potential w(z), whose level curves are equipotentials and field lines. Conformal maps, including Schwarz–Christoffel, carry a solved geometry into edges, slots and fringing-field capacitors. It is the same tool used for 2D potential flow.

name: Kramers–Kronig: causality makes ε(ω) analytic
summary: Polarization cannot come before the field that causes it, so the susceptibility is analytic in the upper half ω-plane. The dispersive and absorptive parts of ε(ω) are then Hilbert transforms of each other. Lorentz-oscillator models satisfy this; conductors need the DC-conductivity pole treated separately. Kronig (1926) and Kramers (1927) first derived the relations for the dispersion of light and X-rays.

name: Legendre generating function is the multipole expansion
summary: Expanding the Coulomb kernel 1/|r−r'| in powers of r_</r_> generates the Legendre polynomials, and the addition theorem turns them into spherical harmonics. Multipole moments are just the source's expansion coefficients in these eigenfunctions of the angular Laplacian.

name: Huygens–Fresnel principle as a Green's-function integral
summary: Kirchhoff diffraction comes from applying Green's theorem to the Helmholtz equation with the outgoing Green's function e^{ikr}/r. This turns Huygens' secondary wavelets into an exact representation. Kirchhoff's boundary conditions are inconsistent, which the Rayleigh–Sommerfeld Dirichlet Green's function repairs. Fresnel and Fraunhofer diffraction are its paraxial and far-field limits.

name: Waveguide and cavity modes as Sturm–Liouville eigenproblems
summary: In a hollow metal guide the longitudinal field obeys the transverse Helmholtz equation, with Dirichlet conditions for TM modes (E_z=0) and Neumann conditions for TE modes (∂_nH_z=0). The eigenvalues set the cutoff frequencies. The complete orthogonal eigenfunctions are the modes into which any guided field expands, like a drum head.

name: Retarded potentials from the wave-equation Green's function
summary: In Lorenz gauge each potential obeys a sourced wave equation, so V and A are ρ and J convolved with the retarded Green's function of the d'Alembertian. Causality selects G_ret over G_adv. Coulomb gauge trades this for an instantaneous Poisson Green's function for V.
map: \Box A^\mu=\mu_0J^\mu,\ G_{\rm ret}=\frac{\delta(t-t'-|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|/c)}{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}

name: Statics as Poisson problems for V and A
summary: Electrostatics, and magnetostatics in Coulomb gauge, both reduce to Poisson equations: one for V and one for each Cartesian component of A. Coulomb's law and the Biot–Savart law are therefore both the sources convolved with the same Green's function 1/(4πr).
map: \nabla^2V=-\rho/\epsilon_0,\ \nabla^2\mathbf A=-\mu_0\mathbf J\Rightarrow\mathbf A=\mu_0\int G\,\mathbf J\,d^3r',\ G=\frac{1}{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r'|}

name: Coulomb potential as the Laplacian's Green's function
summary: The point-charge potential is the free-space Green's function of the Laplacian. Dirichlet and Neumann Green's functions, the method of images and separation of variables (via Sturm–Liouville completeness) are the general PDE tools applied to conductors. Uniqueness follows from the elliptic type of the problem.

name: Liénard–Wiechert fields and Dirac's radiation reaction
summary: Evaluating the retarded Green's function on a point charge's worldline gives the Liénard–Wiechert potentials; the 1−n̂·β factor is the Jacobian of the retarded-time delta function. Dirac took the radiation-reaction field to be half the retarded minus half the advanced field, a combination that is regular at the charge.
map: V=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{(1-\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\boldsymbol\beta)R}\right]_{\rm ret},\quad F_{\rm rad}=\tfrac12(F_{\rm ret}-F_{\rm adv})
sources: Dirac (1938). "Classical theory of radiating electrons". *Proc. R. Soc. A* 167, 148. [doi:10.1098/rspa.1938.0124](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0124)
